name: Burnt Red
lede: Burnt Red is a deep, brownish red, named for the way heat turns earth pigments redder and darker.

sections.title: The name
sections.body:
The name appears in several systems: Ridgway's atlas of 1912, ISCC-NBS block 26 and Maerz and Paul, who date it to 1782 [1]. The swatch sits near brick and [[sienna]] [1].

The heat in the name is real. The Pigment Compendium notes that the Romans knew how to burn yellow ochre into red ochre, and Pliny's sandyx was a burnt red ochre adulterated with white lead [3]. Red ochres of this kind turn up in Roman art and in Byzantine icons and frescoes [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Burnt Red appears in 1.46% of the 23,781 paintings in our archive, as photographed [2]. It peaks in the 1400s at 5.3% of that century's paintings, 3.1 times the baseline [2]. Inside a painting it is nearly always an accent, in 92% of cases [2]. The painter who uses it most is Raphael, in 4 of 36 works here, though none stands out against the baseline [2]. It often shares canvases with Seal Brown [2].

origin.named_after: burning earth pigments; origin of the exact name undocumented
